name: 8-Bit Sidekick
summary: Pulse as a pixel-art sidekick: metrics are platforms, the checkout block crumbles, a red ‘!’ pops and Player 1 chooses ROLL BACK.
look: Dark 8-bit night palette with teal and coral pixels, crisp-edge sprites, double-bordered RPG dialog boxes and big mono HUD numbers with hard pixel shadows.

components.name: Pixel sprite
components.role: Pulse: 12×12 teal critter with a coral antenna dot, 3 poses (idle, wide-eyed, happy)

components.name: Alert ‘!’
components.role: red exclamation over the head = the moment of detection

components.name: Metric platforms
components.role: each metric is a column you can stand on; the anomaly crumbles

components.name: Dialog / choice box
components.role: double-bordered RPG box; the human picks ROLL BACK or ACKNOWLEDGE

components.name: Player 1 sprite
components.role: the human teammate; always the one who makes the decision

motion.name: Stepped frames
motion.how: every sprite animates on 2s at 12 fps (no tweening); pose swaps land exactly on 8th notes (0.25 s at 120 BPM)

motion.name: Alert pop
motion.how: ‘!’ appears in 2 frames (scale 0→1.3→1, steps(2)) with a square-wave blip on the backbeat

motion.name: Typewriter box
motion.how: dialog text reveals 3 characters per frame, pauses on punctuation; box opens with a 4-frame vertical wipe on the bar downbeat

story: Hook: a lost player in a maze of 38 dashboard rooms, 'How many dashboards did you check today?' in a dialog box. Reveal: 'PLAYER 2 HAS JOINED' and Pulse lands under the ACME PULSE logo. Proof: the checkout platform crumbles (−18% since 09:42 after deploy #2231), a red '!' pops over Pulse, the player picks ROLL BACK. CTA: STAGE CLEAR, resolved in 6 min, 'You ship. Pulse watches.' and a START FREE button.
adapt: Turn your product’s objects (metrics, tickets, builds, orders) into platforms or rooms, keep one sprite as your agent, and put your real primary action in the choice box.

references.note: the red ‘!’ alert over a character’s head as instant ‘detected’ grammar
what sprites are and how 8-bit hardware drew them

fit.risk: Retro-game nostalgia can feel gimmicky for serious buyers and pixel text is hard to read small — keep the data box big, use mono with pixel shadows rather than a bitmap font.
